message:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.
response:
Happy to help, and well done for taking it on. Here's everything in order.

## What "lippage" means

Lippage is when one tile's edge sits higher than the tile next to it, leaving a little lip or step. You can feel it with your fingers or bare feet, it catches the light badly, and in bad cases it can trip someone.

It matters with your tiles because long rectangular tiles like 30 × 60 cm are often very slightly bowed, higher in the middle than at the ends. If you lay them in a half-offset brick pattern, the high middle of one tile lines up with the lower end of the next, which makes lippage worse. Two easy fixes:
- Offset each row by **a third of a tile** (20 cm) rather than half.
- Use **tile levelling clips**: cheap plastic clips and wedges that pull neighbouring edges flush while the adhesive sets.

## Grout colour for pale grey porcelain

Go for a **mid-grey a shade or two darker than the tile**, often sold as "mid grey" or "silver grey." It hides everyday dirt and footprints far better than white or very light grey, which will look grubby within weeks on a bathroom floor. It also blends in rather than outlining every tile.

If your budget allows, a **stain-resistant or epoxy grout** stays clean much longer. If you use ordinary cement grout, seal it once it's cured.

## Floor before or after the toilet?

**Floor first, then the toilet.** Tiling the whole floor means the toilet sits on a flat finished surface, with no fiddly cuts around the pan. It also means you can replace the toilet in future without a gap in the tiles.

## How many boxes

- Floor area: 2.4 × 1.8 = **4.32 m²**
- Area of one tile: 0.3 × 0.6 = **0.18 m²**
- Tiles needed: 4.32 ÷ 0.18 = **24 tiles**
- Plus 10%: 24 × 1.1 = 26.4, so **27 tiles**
- Boxes of 8: 27 ÷ 8 = 3.4, so **4 boxes (32 tiles)**

**Buy 4 boxes.** Three boxes would give exactly 24 tiles with nothing spare, and the offset pattern will produce cut pieces at the ends of rows. The extra tiles also give you room for a mistake or two, and some to keep for future repairs. Check that all boxes have the **same batch or shade number** printed on them, as shades can vary slightly between batches.

## Message to the neighbours

> Hi both,
>
> Just a quick heads-up that I'll be cutting tiles for our bathroom floor on Saturday morning, so there'll be some noise from the tile cutter for a few hours. I'll aim to start no earlier than 9:30 and get it done as quickly as I can.
>
> Thank you for being so patient with the skip on the drive these last couple of weeks. It's nearly over, I promise!
>
> [Your name]

Change the start time to suit you.

## Three tips for a first floor

1. **Do a dry layout before mixing any adhesive.** Lay the tiles out loose with spacers to plan where cuts fall. Aim for no thin slivers at doorways or along the most visible wall, and shift the whole layout if needed. Ten minutes here saves the most common beginner regrets.
2. **Get the base right.** The floor must be flat, clean, solid and not springy. If it's floorboards, it usually needs plywood or tile backer board screwed down first. Tiles laid on a flexing floor crack, however well you lay them.
3. **Work in small batches and check as you go.** Mix only as much adhesive as you can use in about 20–30 minutes. Butter the back of each large tile thinly as well as spreading adhesive on the floor. Every few tiles, lift one to check it's fully covered underneath, and lay a spirit level across the tiles. It's much easier to fix a problem in the first ten minutes than the next day.

Bonus: cut outside or in a well-ventilated space, wear eye protection, and use a wet cutter or wear a dust mask. Tile dust isn't something you want to breathe.

The videos do make it look easy, but a small room with tiles this size is a very sensible first project. Go slowly, and good luck.
